title: A single formation is likely shorter than the time needed to transform a species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A single formation is likely shorter than the time needed to transform a species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although each geological formation represents a long lapse of years, each is probably short compared with the time required to change one species into another, so a single formation should rarely contain a full graded series between species.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On the Imperfection of the Geological Record

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Although each formation may mark a very long lapse of years, each perhaps is short compared with the period requisite to change one species into another.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IX, “On the Imperfection of the Geological Record”; section “On the absence of intermediate varieties in any one formation”. Scope: geological formations and fossil species durations

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch09-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Formation duration and fossil occurrence are well represented, but transformation time and complete graded series are harder to measure. Tests are informative yet substantially confounded by temporal resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare durations of formations with independently estimated species-transition durations and measure the frequency of within-formation ancestor-descendant morphological series. Predominantly shorter formations and rare complete series support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Speciation duration is hard to estimate independently of fossil sampling.

Formation boundaries and durations vary regionally.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.68
operationalizability: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Formation ages and taxon ranges are public, and the comparison of their durations is feasible with ordinary database queries. Both clocks are distorted by the same incomplete record, so a numerical inequality is only a partial test of whether one formation should contain a graded species series. Adequacy is good in well-dated marine basins and poor for most terrestrial formations.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the duration of individual formations with observed species durations and with molecular estimates of time to speciation. Formations systematically shorter than speciation times would support the claim and the expectation that one formation rarely holds a full graded series; formation durations as long as species transformations would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A formation can be short and still capture a rapid local transition.

Molecular speciation intervals and fossil durations measure different things.

Observed species durations are truncated and extended by sampling, so they are a biased clock for speciation.
